I'm reading The Eye of the World, by Robert Jordan, for the first time and so far I'm liking it. The characters are well-written, the setting is described nicely and the plot is paced decently. I'm getting a lot of similarities to Tolkien, chiefly in the naming language Jordan is using. "Shayol Ghul," "Andor," and others. What are your thoughts about this book and the series as a whole?
What are your thoughts on the Wheel of Time series?

I enjoyed the series as a whole. Some books were slower than others, but it came together nicely in the end, and it was nice watching the characters develop over time. I have a soft spot for very long series.
I've gotten lots of recommendations from friends to read it, and it sounds like they were right. I'm definitely looking forward to reading them all!

I enjoyed the Wheel of Time as a whole, but a series of this length definitely falls into ruts at various points. Robert Jordan's (and Brandon Sanderson's) writing is good, but not quite up to par with other fantasy authors that I've read. Where the series succeeds is in the setting and its different take on magic, but you will mostly like grow tired of certain important supporting characters that don't seem to grow with the story. The handoff to Sanderson after Jordan's death marks a significant improvement in battle scenes, but Sanderson doesn't capture the previous feel and direction of a couple characters; the most notable of these issues is with Mat (and one of the things that made Towers of Midnight so hard to read). I do highly recommend continuing with the series if you're enjoying the first book, but be careful of anyone who gives the Wheel of Time a 4.5/5 or above, as it definitely has its flaws.

Also, Winter's Heart is easily the slowest point in the series, but it leads into Crossroads of Twilight which is one of my personal favorites. If you make it that far and find that section to be painful, just keep pushing as the story picks up pace again and won't let off through the end of the series.

This is a pretty good summary, although I personally enjoyed the Sanderson portions way more than the Jordan books. I feel like Sanderson was able to explore the world's magic system at a depth that Mr. Jordan never came near.

The middle books, aka the latter of Mr. Jordan's books, dragged something fierce. The beginning and ending books are far superior.

Also, the series is definitely more clear-cut in good vs. evil. I'm glad I read WoT before starting ASOIAF. It would have been very off-putting doing it the other way.

See, I kinda didn't like how Matrim and even Rand haven't really seemed to have change a whole lot towards the end of the first book. I do think that it's because the series is meant to be long and progress a little slowly, but I like when characters progress in noticeable ways throughout each installment. Sort of like an episodic lesson they take in, constantly changing little by little. At the end of the Eye of the World, I almost feel like the characters could have been transplanted from any point in the plot and been nearly the same.

I like the characters, most of them, anyways. A part of me just wishes that they would learn their lessons a little faster.

I really liked the series, but I don't think I'd ever re-read it. And I re-read lots of my favorite books.

Let me amend that a bit actually, I'd read books 1-6 again, refresh myself on plots and goings on for books 7-12 and then re-read 13-15. All the while I'd be pulling my braid and wondering why men and women just don't see eye to eye.

I do think it's worth a read if you like this kind of epic in scope fantasy without all the standard fantasy races via Tolkien. But you will suffer through a lot of world building and character angst. When Sanderson took over the writing of the last books, two things happened. The pacing picked up quite a bit and a lot of loose ends were tied up nicely.

I love Brandon Sanderson. The Way of Kings is a magnificent fantasy work, and Words of Radiance is just as good. Love that author. He's actually one of the reasons I decided to read the Wheel of Time. He and Jordan collaborated on several books, which I found out through a friend. Guy is a such a good author he can end another one's series.

I powered through the first five or six books, several years ago. It felt like the author did a great job building of tension towards an epic climax, but as the series went on, every book seemed to resemble the last, and the plot would stall for hundreds of pages at a time with no development. Eventually I went back to Eddings, who might tell the same story over and over, but, damnit, at least he's finished it a couple of times (RIP, Dave).

I wish I could say I got to meet him personally, but that was not the case. Since that time, much has changed. We lost James Doohan, we lost DeForest Kelley, and we lost Leonard Nimoy.

My childhood heroes may no longer be among us, but their memory lives on.
